title: Eridu
summary: Eridu (Tell Abu Shahrain) in southern Iraq is traditionally the first city of Sumer, where the god Enki had his main temple, rebuilt repeatedly over thousands of years. Excavators trace its origins to the sixth millennium BCE; it is part of the Ahwar of Southern Iraq World Heritage property.

uncertainty.note: Start: the Iraq (2026) paper says early origins in the sixth millennium BC; National Geographic dates the Ubaid period 5300-3800 BC. End: World History Encyclopedia says abandoned around 600 BCE; the Iraq paper says occupied into the first millennium BC. Sources differ and the end is approximate.

as_recorded.value: Eridu itself has early origins in the sixth millennium B.C.

when.display: Settled from the 6th millennium BCE; occupied into the 1st millennium BCE

where.modern_name: Tell Abu Shahrain (Eridu), Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq
where.historical_name: Eridu, Sumerian city of the god Enki, southern Mesopotamia

importance.justification: Traditionally the earliest Sumerian city and long-lived sanctuary of Enki, one of three archaeological components of a UNESCO property.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the dates: World History Encyclopedia gives both c. 5400 and c. 5000 BCE for founding, so I used only the scholarly sixth-millennium statement; its abandonment c. 600 BCE is a single source. The UNESCO XML lists seven unnamed points for property 1481 and I took the one at 30.817 N, 45.996 E as Eridu by position.
